# Rust API Guidelines

> **Source:** [Rust API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/)
>
> Library API design guidelines from the Rust library team. IDs are the upstream `C-XXX` IDs; this table doubles as the checklist.

## [Naming](01-naming.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-CASE](01-naming.md#c-case) | Casing conforms to RFC 430 | Names **SHOULD** follow the basic Rust naming conventions of [RFC 430](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/0430-finalizing-naming-conventions.md): `UpperCamelCase` for "type-level" constructs (types and traits), `snake_case` for "value-level" constructs. |
| [C-CONV](01-naming.md#c-conv) | Ad-hoc conversions follow `as_`, `to_`, `into_` conventions | Conversions **SHOULD** be provided as methods whose name prefix reflects cost and ownership: |
| [C-GETTER](01-naming.md#c-getter) | Getter names follow Rust convention | With a few exceptions, getters **SHOULD NOT** use the `get_` prefix. |
| [C-ITER](01-naming.md#c-iter) | Methods on collections that produce iterators follow `iter`, `iter_mut`, `into_iter` | Per [RFC 199](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/0199-ownership-variants.md), for a container with elements of type `U`, iterator methods **SHOULD** be named `iter` (yields `&U`), `iter_mut` (yields `&mut U`) and `into_iter` (yields `U`). |
| [C-ITER-TY](01-naming.md#c-iter-ty) | Iterator type names match the methods that produce them | A method called `into_iter()` **SHOULD** return a type called `IntoIter`, and similarly for all other methods that return iterators. |
| [C-FEATURE](01-naming.md#c-feature) | Feature names are free of placeholder words | A [Cargo feature](http://doc.crates.io/manifest.html#the-features-section) name **MUST NOT** include words that convey zero meaning, as in `use-abc` or `with-abc`; name the feature `abc` directly. |
| [C-WORD-ORDER](01-naming.md#c-word-order) | Names use a consistent word order | Names **SHOULD** use a word order consistent within the crate and with similar functionality in the standard library; the particular order chosen is not important. |

## [Interoperability](02-interoperability.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-COMMON-TRAITS](02-interoperability.md#c-common-traits) | Types eagerly implement common traits | Crates that define new types **SHOULD** eagerly implement all applicable common traits. |
| [C-CONV-TRAITS](02-interoperability.md#c-conv-traits) | Conversions use the standard traits `From`, `AsRef`, `AsMut` | Conversions **SHOULD** implement [`From`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.From.html), [`TryFrom`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.TryFrom.html), [`AsRef`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.AsRef.html) and [`AsMut`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.AsMut.html) where it makes sense. [`Into`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.Into.html) and [`TryInto`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.TryInto.html) **SHOULD NOT** be implemented. |
| [C-COLLECT](02-interoperability.md#c-collect) | Collections implement `FromIterator` and `Extend` | Collections **SHOULD** implement [`FromIterator`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.FromIterator.html) and [`Extend`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/iter/trait.Extend.html). |
| [C-SERDE](02-interoperability.md#c-serde) | Data structures implement Serde's `Serialize`, `Deserialize` | Types that play the role of a data structure **SHOULD** implement [`Serialize`](https://docs.serde.rs/serde/trait.Serialize.html) and [`Deserialize`](https://docs.serde.rs/serde/trait.Deserialize.html). |
| [C-SEND-SYNC](02-interoperability.md#c-send-sync) | Types are `Send` and `Sync` where possible | Types **SHOULD** be [`Send`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Send.html) and [`Sync`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/marker/trait.Sync.html) where possible. In types that manipulate raw pointers, the `Send`/`Sync` status **MUST** accurately reflect the type's thread-safety characteristics. |
| [C-GOOD-ERR](02-interoperability.md#c-good-err) | Error types are meaningful and well-behaved | Every error type (any `E` in a `Result<T, E>` returned by a public function of the crate) **SHOULD** implement [`std::error::Error`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/error/trait.Error.html), `Send` and `Sync`. `()` **MUST NOT** be used as an error type, even where the error carries no useful information. |
| [C-NUM-FMT](02-interoperability.md#c-num-fmt) | Binary number types provide `Hex`, `Octal`, `Binary` formatting | Any number type on which you would consider bitwise manipulations like `\|` or `&` **MUST** implement [`std::fmt::UpperHex`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.UpperHex.html), [`std::fmt::LowerHex`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.LowerHex.html), [`std::fmt::Octal`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Octal.html) and [`std::fmt::Binary`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/trait.Binary.html). |
| [C-RW-VALUE](02-interoperability.md#c-rw-value) | Generic reader/writer functions take `R: Read` and `W: Write` by value | Generic reader/writer functions **SHOULD** accept `R: Read` / `W: Write` by value, and their docs **MUST** briefly remind users that a mut reference can be passed. |

## [Macros](03-macros.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-EVOCATIVE](03-macros.md#c-evocative) | Input syntax is evocative of the output | Macro input syntax **SHOULD** stay familiar and cohesive with the rest of users' code by mirroring existing Rust syntax where possible, especially the keywords and punctuation that appear in the macro's output. |
| [C-MACRO-ATTR](03-macros.md#c-macro-attr) | Item macros compose well with attributes | Macros that produce more than one output item **SHOULD** support adding attributes to any one of those items. Macros that produce a struct or enum **SHOULD** support attributes so the output can be used with derive. |
| [C-ANYWHERE](03-macros.md#c-anywhere) | Item macros work anywhere that items are allowed | Item macros **SHOULD** work as well as ordinary items everywhere items are allowed (module level and tighter scopes like a function). The test suite **SHOULD** invoke the macro in at least module scope and function scope. |
| [C-MACRO-VIS](03-macros.md#c-macro-vis) | Item macros support visibility specifiers | Items produced by a macro **MUST** follow Rust visibility syntax: private by default, public if `pub` is specified. |
| [C-MACRO-TY](03-macros.md#c-macro-ty) | Type fragments are flexible | A macro accepting a type fragment like `$t:ty` **SHOULD** work with all of: primitives (`u8`, `&str`), relative paths (`m::Data`), absolute paths (`::base::Data`), upward relative paths (`super::Data`) and generics (`Vec<String>`). |

## [Documentation](04-documentation.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-CRATE-DOC](04-documentation.md#c-crate-doc) | Crate level docs are thorough and include examples | Crate-level documentation **SHOULD** be thorough and include examples, as described in [RFC 1687](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/1687). |
| [C-EXAMPLE](04-documentation.md#c-example) | All items have a rustdoc example | Every public module, trait, struct, enum, function, method, macro and type definition **SHOULD** have an example that exercises the functionality, applied within reason. |
| [C-QUESTION-MARK](04-documentation.md#c-question-mark) | Examples use `?`, not `try!`, not `unwrap` | Fallible example code **SHOULD** propagate errors with `?`, not `try!` and not `unwrap`. |
| [C-FAILURE](04-documentation.md#c-failure) | Function docs include error, panic, and safety considerations | Error conditions **SHOULD** be documented in an "Errors" section, panic conditions in a "Panics" section, and unsafe functions **SHOULD** have a "Safety" section explaining all invariants the caller is responsible for upholding to use the function correctly. |
| [C-LINK](04-documentation.md#c-link) | Prose contains hyperlinks to relevant things | Documentation prose **SHOULD** hyperlink to relevant things, as officially recommended by RFC 1574 under ["Link all the things"](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/1574-more-api-documentation-conventions.md#link-all-the-things). |
| [C-METADATA](04-documentation.md#c-metadata) | Cargo.toml includes all common metadata | The `[package]` section of `Cargo.toml` **SHOULD** include `authors`, `description`, `license`, `repository`, `keywords` and `categories`. `documentation` and `homepage` are optional. |
| [C-RELNOTES](04-documentation.md#c-relnotes) | Release notes document all significant changes | Release notes **SHOULD** summarize what changed in each published release, and a link to them (or the notes themselves) **SHOULD** be included in the crate-level docs and/or the repository linked in Cargo.toml. Breaking changes (as defined in [RFC 1105](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/1105-api-evolution.md)) **SHOULD** be clearly identified. |
| [C-HIDDEN](04-documentation.md#c-hidden) | Rustdoc does not show unhelpful implementation details | Rustdoc **SHOULD** include everything users need to use the crate fully and nothing more; implementation details **SHOULD NOT** be real entries in the documentation (explaining relevant ones in prose is fine). |

## [Predictability](05-predictability.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-SMART-PTR](05-predictability.md#c-smart-ptr) | Smart pointers do not add inherent methods | Smart pointer types **MUST NOT** add inherent methods that take `self`; define such operations as associated functions called with the type path (e.g. `Box::into_raw(b)`). |
| [C-CONV-SPECIFIC](05-predictability.md#c-conv-specific) | Conversions live on the most specific type involved | Conversions between two types **SHOULD** live on the more specific type (the one adding an invariant or interpretation the other lacks). When in doubt, you **SHOULD** prefer `to_`/`as_`/`into_` over `from_`. |
| [C-METHOD](05-predictability.md#c-method) | Functions with a clear receiver are methods | Any operation clearly associated with a particular type **SHOULD** be a method on that type rather than a free function taking it as a parameter. |
| [C-NO-OUT](05-predictability.md#c-no-out) | Functions do not take out-parameters | A function returning multiple values **SHOULD** return them via a compound type (tuple or struct) rather than through `&mut` out-parameters. |
| [C-OVERLOAD](05-predictability.md#c-overload) | Operator overloads are unsurprising | Operators with built-in syntax (`*`, `\|`, ...) provided via the [`std::ops`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/index.html#traits) traits **MUST** be implemented only for operations that resemble the operator's usual meaning and share its expected properties. |
| [C-DEREF](05-predictability.md#c-deref) | Only smart pointers implement `Deref` and `DerefMut` | `Deref` and `DerefMut` **SHOULD** be implemented only by smart pointers. |
| [C-CTOR](05-predictability.md#c-ctor) | Constructors are static, inherent methods | Constructors **SHOULD** be static (no `self`) inherent methods on the type they construct, and `new` **SHOULD** generally be the name of the primary constructor. |

## [Flexibility](06-flexibility.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-INTERMEDIATE](06-flexibility.md#c-intermediate) | Functions expose intermediate results to avoid duplicate work | When a function that answers a question also computes related data that is potentially of interest to the client, you **SHOULD** consider exposing that data in the API. |
| [C-CALLER-CONTROL](06-flexibility.md#c-caller-control) | Caller decides where to copy and place data | A function that requires ownership of an argument **SHOULD** take it by value rather than borrowing and cloning it. A function that does not require ownership **SHOULD** take a shared or exclusive borrow rather than taking ownership and dropping the argument. |
| [C-GENERIC](06-flexibility.md#c-generic) | Functions minimize assumptions about parameters by using generics | Functions **SHOULD** use generics to pinpoint exactly the assumptions they need about their arguments; e.g. a function that only iterates over data should take `I: IntoIterator<Item = T>` rather than `&[T]`, `&Vec<T>`, or a specific collection. |
| [C-OBJECT](06-flexibility.md#c-object) | Traits are object-safe if they may be useful as a trait object | When designing a trait, you **MUST** decide early whether it will be used as an object or as a generic bound. A trait meant to be used as an object **SHOULD** have methods that take and return trait objects rather than use generics. |

## [Type safety](07-type-safety.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-NEWTYPE](07-type-safety.md#c-newtype) | Newtypes provide static distinctions | You **SHOULD** use newtypes to statically distinguish between different interpretations of the same underlying type. |
| [C-CUSTOM-TYPE](07-type-safety.md#c-custom-type) | Arguments convey meaning through types, not `bool` or `Option` | Arguments **SHOULD** use a deliberate type (enum, struct, or tuple) that conveys interpretation and invariants, rather than core types like `bool`, `u8` or `Option` that have many possible interpretations. |
| [C-BITFLAG](07-type-safety.md#c-bitflag) | Types for a set of flags are `bitflags`, not enums | When an API's input is the presence or absence of a set of flags, the type **SHOULD** be a [`bitflags`](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags) type, not an `enum`. |
| [C-BUILDER](07-type-safety.md#c-builder) | Builders enable construction of complex values | If constructing a data structure `T` needs many inputs, compound data (e.g. slices), optional configuration, or a choice between several flavors (which leads to many constructors with many arguments), you **SHOULD** consider introducing a `T` builder. |

## [Dependability](08-dependability.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-VALIDATE](08-dependability.md#c-validate) | Functions validate their arguments | Rust code **SHOULD** enforce the validity of its input whenever practical, rather than following the [robustness principle](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robustness_principle) ("be conservative in what you send; be liberal in what you accept"). |
| [C-DTOR-FAIL](08-dependability.md#c-dtor-fail) | Destructors never fail | Destructors **MUST NOT** fail. Instead, provide a separate method for checking clean teardown (e.g. `close`) that returns a `Result` to signal problems. |
| [C-DTOR-BLOCK](08-dependability.md#c-dtor-block) | Destructors that may block have alternatives | Destructors **SHOULD NOT** invoke blocking operations; consider providing a separate method that prepares for an infallible, nonblocking teardown. |

## [Debuggability](09-debuggability.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-DEBUG](09-debuggability.md#c-debug) | All public types implement `Debug` | All public types **SHOULD** implement `Debug`. |
| [C-DEBUG-NONEMPTY](09-debuggability.md#c-debug-nonempty) | `Debug` representation is never empty | The `Debug` representation **SHOULD NOT** ever be empty, even for conceptually empty values. |

## [Future proofing](10-future-proofing.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-SEALED](10-future-proofing.md#c-sealed) | Sealed traits protect against downstream implementations | A trait meant to be implemented only within its defining crate **SHOULD** use the sealed trait pattern, and its rustdoc **SHOULD** state that it is sealed and not meant to be implemented outside the current crate. |
| [C-STRUCT-PRIVATE](10-future-proofing.md#c-struct-private) | Structs have private fields | Struct fields **SHOULD** be private, with getter/setter methods where needed. Public fields are most appropriate for C-spirit `struct` types: compound, passive data structures. |
| [C-NEWTYPE-HIDE](10-future-proofing.md#c-newtype-hide) | Newtypes encapsulate implementation details | You **SHOULD** use a newtype to hide representation details (e.g. a compound iterator type) while making precise promises to the client. |
| [C-STRUCT-BOUNDS](10-future-proofing.md#c-struct-bounds) | Data structures do not duplicate derived trait bounds | Generic data structures **SHOULD NOT** use trait bounds that can be derived or that do not otherwise add semantic value. |

## [Necessities](11-necessities.md)

| ID | Title | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [C-STABLE](11-necessities.md#c-stable) | Public dependencies of a stable crate are stable | A crate **MUST NOT** be declared stable (>=1.0.0) unless all of its public dependencies are stable. |
| [C-PERMISSIVE](11-necessities.md#c-permissive) | Crate and its dependencies have a permissive license | Crates needing maximum compatibility with the Rust ecosystem are **RECOMMENDED** to dual-license under [MIT](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/LICENSE-MIT) OR [Apache 2.0](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/LICENSE-APACHE), like the Rust project. A permissively-licensed crate **SHOULD** generally depend only on permissively-licensed crates. |
